lesson.title: Speakers: Turning an Audio Signal Back Into Sound
lesson.summary: A speaker is a transducer that does the reverse of a microphone, converting the electrical power of an audio signal into the mechanical motion of a diaphragm, which pushes on the air to recreate sound.
lesson.body:
Where a microphone converts sound into an audio signal, a speaker converts an audio signal back into sound, and it does so using electrical power delivered to the speaker's terminals. The most common design, the moving coil, or dynamic, speaker, attaches a coil of wire, the voice coil, to a cone shaped diaphragm, with the coil sitting inside a fixed magnetic field from a permanent magnet. When the audio signal's current flows through the voice coil, the magnetic field exerts a force on the coil, the same Lorentz force that underlies electric motors, pushing the coil, and the attached cone, back and forth in step with the signal. That physical motion of the cone pushes on the surrounding air, recreating the original sound pressure wave.

A speaker's electrical behavior at audio frequencies is often approximated as a fixed resistance, commonly 8 ohms for many consumer speakers, and the power the speaker's voice coil dissipates, converting part of it into sound, follows the same power formula as any resistor, P = V squared divided by R. Audio engineers commonly use a reference of 2.83 volts RMS applied to an 8 ohm speaker specifically because it delivers very close to 1 watt: P = (2.83) squared divided by 8 = 8.0089 divided by 8 = 1.001 watts. That is why speaker sensitivity is so often specified in decibels of sound output at 1 watt, 1 meter using a 2.83 volt reference signal: it is simply the input voltage that produces almost exactly 1 watt into a standard 8 ohm load.

A speaker cannot be specified by voltage alone, because two speakers with different resistances draw different currents, and therefore different power, from the same voltage. That is why the power concept, not just voltage, is essential to describing a speaker's behavior: the sound output depends on how much electrical power is actually converted into mechanical motion of the diaphragm, which is set by both the audio signal's voltage and the speaker's own resistance.
